materials.title: Reading for a seminar
body: Read once for the author's question, then again for the answer they defend. Mark the sentence where the conclusion appears.
Write three objections in your own words. An objection names a reason the conclusion might fail, not a feeling that the chapter was difficult.
Bring one passage you can explain without the book in front of you. That passage is the one you actually understood.

materials.title: Using sources
body: A source supports a claim you are making. It does not replace the claim. Say what you are using it to show.
Quote a sentence when the wording matters. Paraphrase when the point matters more than the wording, and still name the source.
If two sources disagree, describe the disagreement before you take a side. The reader should see what is in dispute.

materials.title: Problem sets
body: Start with the part you can do. A complete easy part is more useful than a blank page waiting for a perfect method.
Write the definition you are using before the calculation. Many wrong answers come from solving a nearby question.
When you check an answer, check the units, the sign, and whether the result is a possible size. Those three catches find different mistakes.

plan.text: Write the deadlines you can already see for the next two weeks.
Read one assigned source and write the author's conclusion in a sentence.
Bring one precise question to a class or a discussion.
Look back at one marked piece of work and name the comment you will use next time.
